extracted.intended_audience: researchers, science journalists, university press officers, and science communicators interested in accuracy of health-related press releases and news
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and outcome measures for identifying exaggeration in health-related academic press releases and the corresponding news coverage, used in a retrospective quantitative content analysis. Focuses on three types of exaggeration (advice, causal claims, and inference from animal studies) and on news uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerated advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice to readers to change behaviour that went beyond those in the associated peer reviewed papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalised as press releases containing advice to change behaviour not supported by the underlying research paper. In the study sample, 40% (95% CI 33% to 46%) of press releases contained exaggerated advice. When press releases contained such exaggeration, 58% (95% CI 48% to 68%) of news stories contained similar exaggeration versus 17% (10% to 24%) when press releases were not exaggerated. Use comparison to the original paper as the reference standard; count as exaggeration only if the press release adds or amplifies behavioural advice beyond the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerated causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Causal statements drawn from correlational research (i.e., asserting causation where the paper reports only correlation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag as exaggeration when the press release asserts or implies a causal relationship that the peer-reviewed study (e.g., observational/correlational design) does not support. In the dataset, 33% (26% to 40%) of press releases contained exaggerated causal claims. When present in press releases, 81% (70% to 93%) of news stories had similar exaggeration compared with 18% (9% to 27%) when the press release was not exaggerated. High odds ratios indicate strong association between press-release causal overstatement and news overstatement. Scoring should evaluate the study design reported in the paper and whether causal language in the release is justified by that design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerated inference to humans from animal research
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference to humans from animal research that went beyond those in the associated peer reviewed papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered an exaggeration when a press release extrapolates animal study findings to human implications or recommendations beyond what the original paper supports. In this study, 36% (28% to 46%) of press releases contained such exaggerated inference. When press releases contained such exaggeration, 86% (77% to 95%) of news stories showed similar exaggeration compared with 10% (0% to 19%) when press releases were not exaggerated. Scoring should compare the species and claims in the paper against the language used in the press release; strong human-directed inference from non-human data is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake (coverage) as outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a press release achieved news uptake (at least one news story) and the mean number of news stories per press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured as presence/absence of any news story referencing the press release and as mean number of news stories. The study found little evidence that exaggeration in press releases increased uptake: the proportion of press releases with some news uptake was not statistically distinguishable regardless of whether the press release contained exaggerated advice, causal statements, or inference to humans from animal research; the mean number of news stories per press release also did not significantly differ with exaggeration. Use these metrics to test whether particular wording strategies affect media pickup.
